1. Introduction
Investigation: A. O. Abubakre
Methodology: M. O. De Kock

Gondwana (Johnson et al., 1996, 2006). During the Permian, an interplay between regional tectonics, an icehouse

Figure 1. Simplified geology of the main Karoo basin of South Africa and locality of borehole KWV-01 (i.e., enlarged inset
from the 1:250,000 3228 Kei Mouth map sheet) shown in relation to published magnetostratigraphic localities (modified from

Polarity Superchron, as a prominent Paleozoic magnetostratigraphic interval, is important. It is an interval of
reverse polarity first described from eastern Australia that extends from ca. 318 to 267–265 Ma, followed by the
Illawarra interval of mixed polarity (Belica, Tohver, Pisarevsky, et al., 2017; Cortrell et al., 2008; Irving, 1963;
Irving & Parry, 1963). The end of the Kiaman Reverse Polarity Superchron (end-Kiaman) is particularly useful as
a chronological marker (Hounslow et al., 2016; Kirschvink et al., 2015). It has been assigned an approximate age
of ∼267 Ma by Steiner (2006) based on data from sedimentary units from North America. In the southwest Karoo
Basin, Lanci et al. (2013) identified normal polarity intervals within the Waterford Formation of the Ecca Group
and the Abrahamskraal Formation of the Beaufort Group, thus placing these rocks in the Illawarra mixed polarity
interval with a mid-Wordian age of ∼269 Ma. This was incorporated in the latest Permian composite magneto-
stratigraphy of Hounslow and Balabanov (2018) (Figure 2). However, Belica, Tohver, Pisarevsky, et al. (2017)
dated normally magnetized volcanic rocks from Australia (i.e., the Gerringong Volcanics) to between 265 and
263.5 Ma. These occur stratigraphically above reversely magnetized interbedded sedimentary and volcanic
units, and therefore constrain the end-Kiaman to coincide with the Wordian-Capitanian boundary at ∼265 Ma
(Figure 2). More recently, Lanci et al. (2022) presented an astronomically calibrated age model from the south-
west Karoo Basin and a 266.5 Ma age for the end-Kiaman.
Here, an integrated rock magnetic and paleomagnetic approach is used to study a 2,353-m-thick intersection
(KWV-01) of the Ecca Group and dolerite intrusions from the southeast main Karoo Basin. The magnetic and
thermal effect of the KLIP intrusions on surrounding sedimentary rocks are characterized and magnetostrati-
graphic constraints are presented for the Ecca Group and lower Beaufort Group to assist lithostratigraphic corre-
lation between extremes of the Karoo Basin. Readers are referred to Akatakpo and Geissman (in press) who
conducted a concurrent and independent paleomagnetic study of the KWV-01 drill core focussing on the effects

of KLIP intrusions. The effects of KLIP intrusions on the Ecca Group are important to evaluate because carbo-
naceous mudstone units of the Ecca Group have been identified as a potential shale-gas resource (Decker, 2014;
Decker & Marot, 2012; Kuuskraa et al., 2013). The scale of this resource, however, is unconstrained and depends,
among other factors, on the lithostratigraphy of the Ecca Group throughout the basin and the thermal effects of
KLIP intrusions (Cole, 2014; De Kock et al., 2017; Mowzer & Adams, 2015).

2. Geological Setting
Basin-fill commences with the glaciogenic Dwyka Group followed by the marine Ecca Group and the
fluvial-deltaic Beaufort Group (Johnson et al., 2006). The subsequent clastic sedimentary sequence of the Storm-
berg Group reflects increasingly arid conditions (Bordy et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 1996) and ends abruptly with
the rapid KLIP dolerite emplacement (Hastie et al., 2014; Jourdan et al., 2005) and eruption of the Drakensberg
Group basalts (Figure 1).
KWV-01 (S 32°14′43.10″ E 28° 35′08.10″) was drilled near Willowvale, within a borrow pit for road aggre-
gate, in the Amathole District of the Eastern Cape Province of South Africa in the southeast extreme of the
main Karoo Basin and within a network of multiple dolerite sills (Figure 1). Bedding in the core is variable, but
generally near horizontal with an average dip to the northwest based on electrical dip meter readings (dip direc-
tion = 302°, dip = 2°; Figure S1 in Supporting Information S2). The core from KWV-01 provides a continuous
2,352.39-m-thick succession from the uppermost layers of the Dwyka Group (i.e., the Elandsvlei Formation,
below 2,331.7 m depth), the entire Ecca Group (subdivided into Prince Albert [2,302.4–2,331.7 m], Whitehill
[2,269.2–2,302.4 m], Collingham [2,002.4–2,269.2 m], Ripon [742.8–2,002.4 m], Fort Brown [262–742.8 m]
and Waterford [241.8–262 m] formations) and the lowermost part of the Beaufort Group (i.e., Koonap Formation
[0–241.8 m], Figure 3). The lithostratigraphy of the Ecca Group here stands in contrast to the southwestern part
of the basin where the Tierberg Formation is developed above the Collingham Formation (Figure 2). The Ripon
Formation, which occurs east of 22° longitude, consists of fine-grained greywacke turbidite beds of varying
thicknesses and is subdivided into the Pluto's Vale Member sandstone (1,388–2,002.4 m), the Wonderfontein
Member shale (948.1–1,388 m), and the Trumpeter's Member sandstone (742.8–948.1 m; Figure 3). Another
marked difference compared to the southwestern part of the basin, is the presence of numerous dolerite intrusions
that intersect the clastic sedimentary rock succession. An 18.82-m-thick fine-grained dolerite intrudes the top of
the Whitehill Formation with a sharp contact in core from KWV-01. The top of this dolerite intrudes sharply
into the base of the 712.14-m-thick arenaceous Pluto's Vale Member of the Rippon Formation. The Pluto's Vale
Member is further intersected six times by dolerite intrusions with a total cumulative thickness of 234.86 m. The
argillaceous Wonderfontein Member is intruded by a 46.07-m-thick dolerite intrusion between 1,249.79 and
1,203.72 m. The Trumpeter's Member envelopes a 9.6-m-thick dolerite intrusion between 965.12 and 955.48 m.
In the upper parts of the core, the Fort Brown Formation is cut by eight thin dolerite intrusions with a total cumu-
lative thickness of 71.75 m, and the Koonap Formation is intruded by two dolerite sills (i.e., 34.87 and 1.87 m
thick) between 127.11 and 92.24 m depth, and between 16.57 and 14.7 m depth.
3. Method
As the KWV-01 core was retrieved, pieces of core were fitted for continuity before being marked by the managing
geologists at the drill site with a reference line indicating the upward direction of the core with an arrowhead (e.g.,
Figures 3d and 4). The orientation line generally coincided with bedding dip azimuth, or in some instances the
up-dip azimuth as seen in the core. The drill-core axis was assumed to be vertical throughout. Where successive
pieces of the core could not be fitted for continuity due to excessive breaking or core loss, the core-section base
was marked by the managing geologists with two short parallel lines perpendicular to the reference line to indi-
cate the end of a continuous section of retrieved core or “core run” (e.g., Figure 3c at 264.25 m, and Figure 4).
A new reference line was then selected and drawn along the next core run. The core is thus made up of several
runs, with pieces of core from the same run being oriented relative to each other (as described by Hailwood and
Ding [1995]). Such core runs ranged from less than a meter to over 100 m (see Figure 3a). The reference line was
drawn to coincide as best as possible with bedding dip azimuths in the core at the start of a specific run by the
managing geologists at the drill site. The actual orientation of the reference line on any run was determined during
sampling and was calculated relative to the bedding dip azimuth as seen in the core and the electrical dip meter
reading at the corresponding depth (i.e., using the closest available dip meter reading to the sampling depth).
Electrical dip meter readings are available at ∼1 m intervals (Figure S1 in Supporting Information S2). Verifi-
cation of the bedding orientation could be made in a few instances by using televiewer imaging of the borehole
wall obtained during a downhole survey after drilling was completed (Figure S2 in Supporting Information S3).
This strategy to determine the orientation of the reference line, however, has significant associated uncertainty
given the low average dip of 2° and wavy bedding surfaces. It was, for example, impossible to distinguish between
bedding dips and depositional dips. Furthermore, electronic dip meter logging was not possible for the first

Figure 4. Workflow for orientation of core plugs. A, B, and C are in the same reference frame marked by X, Y, and Z.
Where X is downward and aligned with the l core axis, which is assumed to be vertical. Y and Z are both in the plane that
is perpendicular to the core axis (i.e., horizontal). (a) Core run marked with continuous reference line indicating the up
direction. Reference lines were drawn by a geological manager at the drill site upon core retrieval, and typically were drawn
to coincide with either the bedding dip direction or the bedding up-dip azimuth seen in the core. The base of core runs was
marked by short double lines perpendicular to the reference line. (b) Core was cut along the reference line with a diamond
saw. Plugs drilled from the halve to the right of the reference line. (c) Plugs were labeled with their depth and a reference
arrow was marked along its upper margin. Reference arrows on plugs are horizontal with azimuth equal to the orientation of
the reference line of the relevant core run minus 90°. (d) The orientation of the reference line (and therefore the arrows on
plugs) for a specific core run were determined relative to the bedding at the relevant depth using the electrical dip meter log
value at the corresponding depth (i.e., spot value).
16 m of the core due to an installed casing, nor was it possible beyond 2,000 m due to hole collapse after core
retrieval. Orientation of the reference line in the first 16 m and beyond 2,000 m is thus subject to even greater
uncertainty. For these sections, the reference line was assumed to correspond with the average bedding azimuth
in the core (i.e., 302°/2°). Despite uncertainties, it was the only available option available to orient the core.
Relative consistency of obtained remanence directions throughout the core attest to some measure of success of
the core orientation attempt. Core logging and sampling were done at the Council for Geosciences National Core
Library at Donkerhoek, South Africa. Plug samples for paleomagnetic analyses were taken at ∼3 m intervals in
general, but this spacing was variable depending on the lithology and the condition of the core. A piece of core
earmarked for sampling was first cut along the reference line by diamond saw before a paleomagnetic sample
was plugged perpendicular to the core axis and always from the right-hand half of the split core using a bench-
top drill press (Figure 4). Plugs were labeled with their depth and a reference arrow was marked along a plug's
upper margin (Figure 4). Plugs were prepared into specimens (one per plug) for step-wise demagnetization at the
paleomagnetism laboratories at the University of Johannesburg (UJ) and the California Institute of Technology
(Caltech). Demagnetization consisted of static axis progressive alternating field (AF) demagnetization in three
to four 2.5 mT steps up to 7.5 or 10 mT. Thermal demagnetization was achieved through stepwise heating in
20–25°C steps from 100 to 600°C. All measurements of remanence were made using 2G Enterprises 755 or
DC-4K superconducting rock magnetometers of specimens in four positions, first in an upward orientation and
then repeated for the specimen in a downward orientation.

Remanence components were identified and quantified via principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980)
using PaleoMag 3.2 (Jones, 2002) with individual components calculated from three or more points for line fits.
Planes were fitted based on four or more points where stable end points of demagnetization were not reached.
Component fits were used in subsequent analysis after application of a data filter to exclude fits with mean angu-
lar deviation (MAD) values ≤ 15° or 20° for line and plane fits, respectively. These data filters aim to objectively
eliminate outliers and unreliable data, and are commonly employed by the paleomagnetic community. Cut-off
values for acceptable MAD values vary between studies but are typically between 10° and 20°, with the cut-off
value for plane fits usually being larger (e.g., Belica, Tohver, Flint, et al., 2017; Belica, Tohver, Pisarevsky,
et al., 2017; Sciscio et al., 2017). Component means were calculated using PaleoMag 3.2. The methodology of
McFadden and McElhinny (1988) for the combination of line and plane fits was employed on data from the whole
core. Final iterative directions along the arc constraints were combined with fitted lines from the whole core for
the calculation of component means and stratigraphic polarity interpretation. Component means from the whole
core were used to calculate virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) as per Butler (1992). The VGPs were visualized
using GPlates 2.2 (Williams et al., 2012). Remanence components interpreted as being primary were used to
develop a magnetostratigraphic record by considering the stratigraphic variation of declination, inclination and
the corresponding VGP latitude (calculated as per Lowrie and Alvarez [1984]).
Off cuts from 14 representative plug samples were subjected to a suite of rock magnetic experiments as described
by Kirschvink et al. (2008). This includes progressive isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition up
to 1,000 mT in a pulse-field followed by progressive static AF demagnetization up to 150 mT, progressive anhy-
steretic remanent magnetization (ARM) acquisition with a direct current biasing field raging up to 1 mT followed
by progressive static AF demagnetization up to 150 mT, an ARM version of the Lowrie-Fuller test (e.g., Johnson
et al., 1975) and a comparison of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) and ARM stability with IRM stability
after Fuller et al. (1988). IRM acquisition curves were unmixed using the MAX Unmix software (Maxbauer
et al., 2016), which employs a skewed log-normal distribution (Wuertz & Chalabi, 2015) to represent individual
coercivity components. Together these rock magnetic methods can be used to distinguish between different ferro-
magnetic minerals based on their observed properties (e.g., Peters & Dekkers, 2003) and assist in interpretation
of demagnetization data.
4. Results
4.1. Rock Magnetic Results
Some partition of magnetic mineralogy is expected in a sandstone-shale succession like that of the KWV-01 core.
Unfortunately, magnetic susceptibility data are not available to visualize this, but a comparison of NRM intensity
and demagnetization intensity after 200°C versus the NRM intensity (i.e., J /J) provides an initial opportunity
200 0
to assess the rock magnetic behavior of samples. The NRM intensities are generally monotonous throughout the
core (Figure 5), with a steady decrease in NRM intensity values with depth (i.e., from around 1 × 10 −3 A/m at
the top of the core, to 1 × 10 −4 A/m at the base of the core). A gamma-ray log of the borehole suggests that the
fine-grained sandstone units have a significant mud component (Figure 5), which likely mutes the difference in
rock magnetic behavior of the mudstone versus the sandstones. Superimposed on the decreasing trend with depth
are increases in NRM intensity by as much as three orders of magnitude around dolerite intrusions (e.g., around
dolerite nos. 2, 4–6, 7, 9, 10, 13, 16, and 17; Figure 5). However, not all dolerites have this effect. There are little
noticeable effects around some thin dolerites like nos. 1, 3, 8, and 15, while dolerites nos. 11 and 14 are associ-
ated with decreases in the NRM intensities of surrounding sedimentary units. In general, NRM intensity dimin-
ishes by about an order of magnitude after demagnetization to 200°C, but samples with elevated NRM intensity
(particularly those around dolerite nos. 2, 4–6, and 16) are demagnetized much faster and loose up to 4 orders of
magnitude after demagnetization to 200°C (Figure 5).
The fine-grained sandstones in general have higher mean destructive fields of IRM, higher remanent coercive
force (H ) values, and higher ratios of SIRM demagnetized to the H value compared to the original SIRM (i.e.,
CR CR
R-ratios after Cisowski, 1980). These variables tend to be slightly lower for mudstones (Table S3 in Supporting
Information S4). Nine of the 14 samples acquire IRM linearly (on a log scale) from 20–30 to 300 mT but only
reach or approach saturation above 600–700 mT (Figure 6a). IRM is acquired more steeply in two mudstone
samples (i.e., 475.14 and 2,245.3) from 20 to 100 mT, and saturation is approached from 200 to 400 mT and
reached by 500 mT (Figure 6b). IRM is acquired non-linearly in three samples (i.e., 191.13, 916.45, and 996.51).

### page_10
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2022JB024384
The samples are of variable lithology and approach saturation at fields only above 700 mT. Steeper acquisition is
seen in the mudstone samples KWV191.13 and KWV996.51 before 100 mT, followed by less steep acquisition
that becomes steeper again after 300 mT (Figure 6c). Sandstone sample KWV916.45 show shallower acquisition
before 100 mT, after which acquisition becomes steeper (Figure 6d).
IRM acquisition curve decomposition identifies six possible components. When fitting such models, a strategy
was followed to keep components within a relatively constant coercivity range throughout the sample set. Each
component is described by its median coercive field, dispersion parameter, relative proportion, and skewness
(Table S3 in Supporting Information S4). Any specific sample requires two, but more commonly three, and
rarely four phases to match the IRM acquisition spectra. Generally, IRM acquisition is dominated by a medium
coercivity or MC1 component (mean coercivity = 122 ± 27 mT; Figure 6e). Samples that reach saturation above
700 mT display small contributions of both low and high coercivity phases (LC1 with a mean coercivity of
26 ± 6 mT; and HC1 with a mean coercivity of 488 ± 51 mT) in addition to the main contribution of MC1, and
in one case there is also a small contribution from a very high coercivity phase (i.e., HC2 with a mean coercivity
of 1,284 ± 401 mT). Samples that reach saturation at 200–400 mT display either low (i.e., LC2 with a mean
coercivity of 51 ± 7 mT) or medium coercivity phases (i.e., MC1) as main contributors to the IRM together with
a small contribution of LC1, but without higher coercivity phases contributing (Figure 6f). Nonlinear IRM acqui-
sition is characterized by either dominant LC2 contributions (in KWV191.13 and KWV996.51; Figure 6g) or by
a dominant medium coercivity (i.e., MC2 with a mean coercivity of 274 ± 47 mT) in KWV916.45 (Figure 6h).
There are additional small contributions of LC1 and MC2 phases in KWV191.13, and by MC2 and HC2 phases
in KWV996.51. Apart from a dominant MC2 phase, a small LC1 contribution is also recognized in the IRM
acquisition by sample KWV916.45.
The Lowrie-Fuller test was originally proposed to distinguish between single-domain (SD) and multi-domain
(MD) remanence. The test is based on the observation that the relative stability thermal remanence (or ARM)
in SD grains against AF demagnetization decreases with an increasing inducing field, while the opposite is true
for MD grains (Johnson et al., 1975; Lowrie & Fuller, 1971). However, the Lowrie-Fuller test has been shown
not be this clear cut and that MD grains can yield a positive Lowrie-Fuller test (Halgedahl, 1998; Newell, 2000;
Xu & Dunlop, 1995). The Lowrie-Fuller test is thus not necessarily a good indicator of domain size and can be
affected by grain volume, grain orientation, stress, particle interaction, and by the distribution of microcoercivity
in a particular sample. An ARM version of the Lowrie-Fuller test (Johnson et al., 1975) shows an L-type response
(i.e., ARM is more stable; Xu & Dunlop, 1995) in all our samples (Figure 7a). This could suggest the dominance
of SD or pseudo-SD particles, but MD grains with L-type responses cannot be excluded. The L-type response of
our samples is encouraging, albeit not an exclusive indicator of paleomagnetic stability.
The ARM acquisition for all the samples confirms variable inter-particle interaction as suggested by R-ratio that
range between 0.29 and 0.46 (Figure 7b). Interaction is highest for KWV231.42, KWV425.45, and KWV475.14
(R-ratio of 0.29–0.39), which resemble ARM acquisition by chiton teeth (Figure 7b; after Kirschvink et al., 2008).
Curves otherwise resemble ARM acquisition by partially collapsed bacterial magnetosomes (Figure 7b; after
Kirschvink et al., 2008). The least inter-particle interactions are seen in KWV2245.3, KWV996.51, KWV916.45,
and KWV191.13 (R-ratio of 0.39–0.46).
The Fuller test uses comparison of NRM:IRM and ARM:IRM to infer if a magnetization is detrital, chemical,
or thermal in origin (Fuller et al., 1988). The test was calibrated for magnetite and can thus only be applied to
samples in which magnetite is a primary ferromagnetic mineral (see Section 5). Multiple magnetic phases compli-
cate interpretation of these curves. Plots of NRM and ARM demagnetization values against IRM demagnetiza-
tion for select samples reveal a conspicuous soft NRM component in most samples that is removed by 10 mT
(Figure 7c). The ratio of NRM to IRMs is generally in the 1:1,000 range for demagnetization between 10 and
50 mT for most specimens, but for four specimens (KWV716.74, KWV916.45, KWV996.51, and KWV1764.7)
the ratio was in the 1:100 range. At higher field levels, the AF demagnetization of NRM proceeds much slower
than the AF demagnetization of IRM, and the curve is characteristically concave upwards for all our specimens.
The ARM behaves similarly, albeit less pronounced. ARM:IRM values are above 0.1 in all specimens and are
equal to, or exceed 1 at demagnetization levels above 70 mT (Figure 7c).

4.2. Demagnetization
4.2.1. Sedimentary Rocks
Four magnetic components were identified during the demagnetization of sedimentary rock specimens (Table 1).
The demagnetization behavior was variable as expected for the range of different lithologies and grain sizes.
The four components were a low coercivity or soft magnetic component (SFT); a variable, but typically north to
northwest directed and moderately steep upward-directed component (A); a northerly and steep upward-directed
high stability magnetization (B−); and a southerly and steep downward directed high stability magnetization
(B+). Any specific specimen, however, recorded a maximum of three components, and many were characterized
by just two components or a single magnetic component (Figure 8).
The demagnetization behavior of nine specimens proved too erratic for the identification of any magnetic compo-
nents, and these are not further considered.
A low coercivity SFT component was identified in 220 of the 400 specimens during AF demagnetization steps
up to low-temperature demagnetization steps (Figures 8a–8f). The SFT component is poorly defined, with MAD
values > 15° for fits from 56 of the specimens. These components are randomly directed and not considered to
be of any geological significance.
After the removal of SFT components, prominent remanence components (i.e., component A) unblocked as either
linear trajectories toward the origin or as linear trajectories that miss the origin to reveal the presence of rema-
nence components of higher thermal stability (Figures 8a–8e). These A components were identified in 311 spec-
imens (plus 34 specimens in which it was identified, but which were excluded due to their >15° MAD values).
The A components are highly variable in terms of their unblocking and direction. They are generally northerly
and upward-directed, but with a very low Fisher precision parameter for the mean direction (k = 5.55; Figure 9a).
The A components unblocks between 340 and 460°C in general.
In specimens where A component trajectories do not demagnetize toward the origin, higher stability components
(B− and B+) are revealed as either stable end-points of demagnetization with linear demagnetization trajectories
toward the origin (e.g., Figure 8b, 8c, and 8e), or more commonly as demagnetization along planes away from

### page_14
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2022JB024384
the A component direction toward the south-east up B+ direction (e.g., Figure 8d). The B− and B+ components
variably unblock between 250 and 520°C, but most commonly unblock above 400°C. B− components were
identified in 65 specimens (plus 2 specimens in which it was identified, but which were excluded due to their
>15° MAD values). The B− components are northerly and upwards directed and often steeper than the A compo-
nents (Figures 9a and 9b). The distribution of B− components appears elongated, but this is likely an artifact of
uncertainties in drill core orientation (see De Kock et al. [2009] for a description of this artifact). B+ components
were most commonly identified as demagnetization along planes away from the A component direction (i.e., in
122 specimens after the exclusion of 10 specimens for which planes had MAD values that were >20°), but also
as components with linear demagnetization trajectories toward the origin after the removal of the SFT and A
components (i.e., in 37 specimens), and rarely (i.e., in 9 specimens) as single remanence components. Like the
B− components, the B+ components also define a slightly elongated distribution (Figure 9c). The B+ component
mean was calculated using either only line fits, or a combination of fitted lines and planes. The methodology of
McFadden and McElhinny (1988) for the combination of line and plane fits was employed on data from the whole
core, so that inferred directions along the arc constraints were combined with lines for calculating the mean.
The B− and B+ components are nearly antipodal, but the line fit data fail the reversal tests of McFadden and
McElhinny (1990) with in-situ remanence directions (Table 1). Upon repeating the same test with tilt-corrected
line fit remanence directions, the data gives a C quality reversals test (Table 1).
4.2.2. Dolerite
Dolerite specimens are characterized by small contributions of SFT components and dominated by northerly up
magnetizations that remain stable above 400°C (i.e., DOL components; Figure 8f). An average for the northerly
up DOL components was calculated from six specimens (Figure 9d).
The extent of the effect of dolerite sills on the surrounding rock is best seen in Figure 5. A steadily decreasing
trend in NRM intensity values with depth display abrupt increases in NRM intensity by as much as three orders
of magnitude around dolerite intrusions due to the growth of new magnetic minerals (e.g., around dolerite nos. 2,
4–6, 7, 9, 10, 13, 16, and 17; Figure 5). There are little noticeable effects around some thin dolerites like nos. 1,
3, 8, and 15, while dolerites nos. 11 and 14 are associated with decreases in the NRM intensities of surrounding
sedimentary units. The effect of individual dolerite intrusions on surrounding sedimentary units was evaluated,
and demagnetization behavior and magnetic components of intrusions and sedimentary units were found to be
strongly contrasting in most cases. For example, multiple sills with a cumulative thickness of ∼60 m intrude
the upper Pluto's Vale Member between 1,680 and 1,740 m depth. Two dolerite specimens (KWV1692.5 and
KWV1717.27) yielded north up DOL components that were stable up to 400°C with minor contributions by
SFT components. Sedimentary rock units immediately above and below the intrusion, however, displayed clear
demagnetization trajectories along planes away from the A components toward the B+ remanence direction.
The A components of specimens surrounding the intrusion are comparable to the DOL direction (Figure 9), and
it appears that the magnetic effects of this intrusion on the surrounding sedimentary units were limited in general
to a few meters above and below the intrusions (Figure 5).
5. Discussion
5.1. Carriers of Remanence
Most mudstone and fine-grained sandstone show a single dominant magnetic phase. Samples generally share a
similar mid-coercivity peak (MC1 around ∼130 mT) with lesser contributions from low and high coercivity phases
(LC1 and HC1/HC2). The LC1 peak at ∼28 mT could represent detrital oxidized magnetite (e.g., Egli, 2003),
Figure 8. Representative demagnetization behavior of selected specimens. (a) KWV546.27 is dominated by an origin-seeking A component as a single magnetic
component. (b) KWV246.53 and (c) KWV283.08 display A components that miss the origin up to ∼350°C before steeper origin-seeking trajectories define the B−
components. KWV246.53 display a small contribution of a SFT component to the remanence, that is, removed by AF demagnetization step at 10 mT. (d) KWV309.1
display small contributions of SFT components after which an A component unblocks as a linear trajectory that misses the origin. AF demagnetization steps are
not shown for KWV309.1 due to misalignment of specimen during AF procedure. At high-temperature demagnetization steps, component B+ is revealed as planes
of demagnetization away from the A component direction to rarely reach stable endpoints of demagnetization, as in the case of (e) KWV460.05. (f) KWV92.38 is
dominated by northeast up DOL component as an origin seeking-trajectory. AF demagnetization steps are not shown for KWV92.38 due to misalignment of specimen
during AF procedure. Zijderveld diagrams: red = inclination data, blue = declination data. Equal-area nets: red = up, blue = down. J/Jo = normalized magnetization.
Additional demagnetization examples are provided as Figure S4 in Supporting Information S1.

### page_16
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2022JB024384
but may also be pyrrhotite (e.g., Martin-Hernández et al., 2008; Peters & Dekkers, 2003). Pyrrhotite may be
responsible for the drops in magnetization seen during the heating of some specimens between 250 and 300°C,
and has also been identified by X-ray diffraction analysis of the mudstones from the Whitehill and Collingham
formations in core KWV-01 (Geel et al., 2021). Unfortunately, that study did not distinguish between monoclinic
and hexagonal pyrrhotite. They also did not include diffractograms in their report. Pyrrhotite, however, is difficult
to identify with the particular suite of room temperature rock magnetic analyses performed here. Other kinds of
magnetizations were not investigated. The contribution by the LC1 phase to the remanence is, however, minimal.
The MC1 peak around ∼130 mT in most of our samples is interpreted as high coercivity titanomagnetite (Peters
& Dekkers, 2003) and the high coercivity phases with peaks above or around 1,000 mT (i.e., HC2) are provi-
sionally identified hematite, as goethite typically only becomes magnetized at much higher fields in IRM (Hu
et al., 2013; Rochette et al., 2005). The HC2 phase is only seen in three samples as a negligible contributor to
IRM. The high coercivity peaks between 444 and 560 mT (i.e., HC1) present in many of the samples is within the
range of very fine-grained detrital hematite (e.g., Swanson-Hysell et al., 2019). HC1 is present in most samples
as a very minor contributor to IRM, and is not considered an important carrier of remanence, because none of the
specimens carried stable magnetizations after demagnetization above 540°C.
Two mudstone samples yielded higher low coercivity peaks at ∼54 mT (i.e., LC2) in combination with
medium-coercivity peaks around ∼130 mT (i.e., MC1) and small peaks at ∼269 mT (i.e., MC2). Both the LC2
and MC1 peaks are interpreted to be magnetite of varying coercivity (e.g., Peters & Dekkers, 2003), with the
LC2 peak dominating the remanence. The higher coercivity peak is within the range expected for hematite (i.e.,
140–800 mT; Hu et al., 2013; Slotznick et al., 2016), and is interpreted as pigmentary hematite (Swanson-Hysell
et al., 2019) with a negligible contribution to the overall remanence.
The dominant magnetic phase in most of the samples is thus interpreted to be magnetite of variable coerciv-
ity. NRM:IRM ratios in most samples are in the 1:1,000 range and are consistent with the NRM largely being
a post-depositional or depositional remanent magnetization (pDRM or DRM). Samples KWV716.74 and
KWV1764.7 have an NRM:IRM ratio in the 1:100 range. Both of these samples have a main coercivity peak
at ∼130 mT and are dominated by magnetite. Magnetization carried in these samples is more likely secondary
magnetizations, possibly a thermal remanent magnetization (TRM) due to the heating effects of dolerite intru-
sions, or a chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) due to diagenetic alteration in response to burial. However,
sample KWV716.74 is not in the vicinity of an intrusion, but does share an elevated NRM intensity with samples
that are associated with intrusions. KWV1764.7 is near a fairly thick dolerite intersection (no. 14) in the core and
is likely baked.
Only three of our test samples displayed remanence dominated by two magnetic phases. These were KWV191.13
and KWV996.51, representing mudstones, and KWV916.45, which is a fine-grained sandstone. These samples
showed both LC1 or LC2 peaks (i.e., low coercivity magnetite/pyrrhotite?) as one dominant phase, and MC1
(high coercivity magnetite) or MC2 (hematite?) peaks as a second dominant phase in combination with smaller
peaks (e.g., HC1 or HC2). For these samples, the Fuller test that shows NRM:IRM ratios between the 1:1,000 and
1:100 range cannot be interpreted easily, as the test was originally calibrated for magnetite.
The pronounced concave upward shape of the NRM:IRM curves suggests that magnetically soft phases (LC1 and
LC2) are not efficient carriers of weak field remanent magnetization. NRM carried in high-coercivity phases are
effectively immune to AF demagnetization up to 100 mT which flattens out the NRM:IRM curves. Pseudo-SD
or SD magnetite or titanomagnetite (±pyrrhotite?) are thus identified as the principal carriers of the A, B+, and
B− remanence components.
5.2. Timing of Remanence Acquisition and Paleopole Calculation
The DOL component seen in the KLIP intrusions is different from the B+ magnetizations revealed during
high-temperature demagnetization steps in the surrounding sedimentary units. The DOL direction is, however,
somewhat comparable to the B− directions (Figure 9), although nowhere in direct association in the core apart
from a few single specimens from within the bakes contact zones of intrusions 4, 7, 10, 14, and 17 (Figure 5).
These may be misidentified and could be construed as the effect of intrusions (i.e., A components that remain
stable to higher thermal demagnetization steps). The DOL direction is also comparable to the lower temperature

Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2022JB024384
Figure 10. (a) The B ±pole from KWV-01 (uncorrected for inclination shallowing) compared to published Ecca Group and Beaufort Group poles and the RM
Gondwana apparent polar wander path of Torsvik et al. (2012) in South African coordinates. (b) The B ±pole corrected for inclination shallowing by a factor of 0.6
compared to the RM f = 0.6 Gondwana apparent polar wander path of Torsvik et al. (2012) in South African coordinates.
A direction that is developed throughout most of the core (Figure 5, Table 1). The DOL direction is distinguisha-
ble from the B− component using 95% confidence, but statistically the same as the A component using the F-test
for comparison of two directions after Butler (1992). The angle between the DOL and B− means is 28.3° and
larger than the critical angle of 20.7° at which the two means would be indistinguishable. The angle between the
DOL and A component means is 20.1° and smaller than the critical angle of 26.3° (at 95% confidence) which
suggests the means are indistinguishable (Butler, 1992). We, therefore, interpret the A component as a remanence
that was acquired during heating by the KLIP dolerite intrusions. The B+ and B− components are interpreted
to be older magnetizations, and likely primary Permian magnetizations recorded as pDRMs or DRMs that pass
a quality C reversal test (for tilt-corrected remanence directions). Paleopoles were calculated for the DOL and
A components based on in-situ remanence directions, and for the B+ and B− components based on remanence
directions after bedding was restored to paleohorizontal.
B−, B+, and their combined paleopoles (Figure 10) are comparable to the 240–180 Ma segment of the Gondwana
reference apparent polar wander path of Torsvik et al. (2012). Our poles are also comparable to the Ecca Group
pole presented for the KZF-01 core from the southwestern Karoo Basin of Abubakre and De Kock (2021) as well
as the upper Beaufort Group poles of De Kock and Kirschvink (2004), but are somewhat different from the poles
reported by Lanci et al. (2013), Tohver et al. (2015), and Belica, Tohver, Flint, et al. (2017), which plots further
to the east from our pole as well as the Gondwana reference apparent polar wander path of Torsvik et al. (2012)
(Figure 10a). Like this study, both Belica, Tohver, Flint, et al. (2017) and Abubakre and De Kock (2021) report
data from drill core. Sample declination is thus expected to be less precise than for studies from outcrop (e.g.,
Lanci et al., 2013; Tohver et al., 2015). This can be seen in the higher dispersion along declination for the
KWV-01 core in Figure 9, but also in the variability of B± declination with depth, which is much higher than
the variability of B± inclination with depth (Figure 11). The larger dispersion in declination values affects the
paleopole calculation, and could explain the difference between paleopoles of similar age.
Another explanation for mismatch between paleopoles might be the variable effect of inclination shallowing.
Correcting for inclination shallowing is typically done through the use of magnetic anisotropy; the DRM tensor
method by Jackson et al. (1991); the Elongation-Inclination (E-I) method by Tauxe and Kent (2004) using the
statistical field model TK03.GAD on a large data set (>100); and a correction method by King (1955) that

### page_18
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2022JB024384
Figure 11. Magnetic polarity interpretation for KWV-01 based on inclination, declination, and VGP latitude stratigraphic variation of the B− and B+ remanence
directions (all in-situ remanence directions).
adopts an empirically derived flattening factors (f) typically between 0.54 and 0.79, and a mean value of 0.65
for magnetite-dominated rocks (Bilardello & Kodama, 2010). Although these approaches are based on certain
assumptions, they have associated advantages and intrinsic limitations in their application for investigating shal-
low inclinations in sedimentary rocks. Since it is relatively difficult to quantify the DRM tensor, and due to the
absence of magnetic anisotropy data set for this study, we opted to explore applying either the E-I method by
Tauxe and Kent (2004) or the (f) factor method by King (1955). The E–I method by Tauxe and Kent (2004) is
relatively easy to apply using PmagPy software (Tauxe et al., 2016), and a large data set is required to adequately
sample paleomagnetic directions resulting from paleosecular variation of the geomagnetic field. Using our B+
data, the E-I method yield and f value of 0.62 (E-I corrected inclination of 74.9° with bootstrapped 95% confi-
dence interval of 66.2°–83.7°). However, this method is described by Li and Kodama (2016) as not well suited for
the successions such as the Karoo successions that are deposited at slow sediment accumulation rates and affected

### page_19
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2022JB024384
by local tectonics (Catuneanu, 2004; Tankard et al., 2009). This limitation is based on the relative vertical-axis
rotations between these sampling sites which leads to the development of an apparent E-W elongation that is
unrelated to inclination shallowing, and a resultant under- or over-corrections for inclination shallowing (Li &
Kodama, 2016). However, KWV-01 represents a single sampling site or locality. Relative vertical-axis rotation
does however result from our core orientation leading to artificial elongation of declination data. However, an
inclination factor of 0.62 is not unexpected for rocks dominated by magnetite (Bilardello & Kodama, 2010).
Lanci et al. (2013) and Tohver et al. (2015) applied the E-I method to correct for inclination shallowing in similar
rocks from the southwest Karoo basin with a corresponding inclination factor of between 0.68 and 0.71. Applica-
tion of an inclination factor of f = 0.6 to our data is thus not considered unreasonable. This factor (f) was used in
an inclination correction equation that considers inclination shallowing as a tangent-tangent relationship:
tan(observedinclination)=f×tan(inclinationatdeposition)
𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡(𝐼𝐼 ) = 𝑓𝑓𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡(𝐼𝐼 ) 𝑂𝑂 𝑓𝑓
and the results yielded a corrected inclination of 77.0°, and a corrected pole at 53.2°S, 46.9°E (Table 1; Figure 10b).
5.3. Magnetostratigraphy and End of the Kiaman Reverse Polarity Superchron in KWV-01
The B− and B+ remanence directions (i.e., line fits as well as inferred directions along the remagnetization-arcs
obtained for the combination of B ±line and plane fits from the method of McFadden and McElhinny (1988))
define stratigraphically bound groupings and can be used to construct a magnetostratigraphy for the KWV-01
core (Figure 11). The core is dominated by reverse polarity magnetozones. Three normal polarity magnetozones
are recorded in the KWV-01 core and are labeled KWV2n, KWV3n, and KWV4n. Normal polarity magnetozone
KWV4n is recorded in the uppermost specimens of the core and within the Koonap Formation. The remainder
of the Koonap Formation, Waterford Formation, and the uppermost Fort Brown Formation define magnetozone
KWV3 between 325 and 20 m depth. It is defined by a prominent normal polarity magnetozone (137–328 m) and
reverse polarity magnetozone (20–137 m). There are possible normal polarity subzones at 82 m depth, but these
are in proximity to an intrusion and could represent the effect of normal magnetized dolerite on the otherwise
reverse magnetized sedimentary rocks at this depth, and are thus regarded as suspect. Several possible reverse
polarity subzones occur within KWV3n. The presence of a normal magnetized dolerite sill within the Koonap
Formation does not affect the resolution of the KWV3r magnetozone. The Fort Brown Formation host one
magnetozone (i.e., KWV2). The KWV2r reverse polarity magnetozone is well-defined between 328 and 446 m
(Figure 11). KWV2n extends to 522 m. The remainder of the core is dominated by a very thick reverse polarity
magnetozone (KWV1r), but two normal polarity subzones are recorded in the lower Fort Brown Formation (i.e.,
KWV1r.3n and KWV1r.2n) and within the Trumpeters Member (i.e., KWV1r.1n). Possible, but poorly defined
normal polarity subzones were identified within the Fort Brown Formation between KWV1r.3n and KWV1r.2n
at ∼600 m and within the Trumpeters Member between KWV1r.1n and KWV1r.2n at 781.5 m. Additional poorly
defined normal polarity subzones occur in the Wonderfontein Member (at 981 m). Other possible normal polarity
subzones are in the Wonderfontein Member (at 1,141 m), the Pluto's Vale Member (at 1,784 m), and at the base
of the Collingham Formation (at 2,259 m). These are proximal to intrusions and could represent the effect of
normal magnetized dolerite on the otherwise reverse magnetized sedimentary rocks. Normal magnetized doler-
ite intrusions within the Wonderfontein Member, the Pluto's Vale Member, the Collingham Formation, and the
Whitehill Formation appear to have little effect on the resolution of the KVWr1 reverse polarity magnetozone,
except for the possible normal polarity subzones. Sample coverage between 1,923 and 2,200 m is poor and this
interval is largely represented by dolerite, so the polarity interpretation for sedimentary units in the interval is
uncertain (Figure 11).
5.4. Magnetostratigraphic Correlation and Geochronology of the Ecca Group Across the Southern
Karoo Basin
The magnetostratigraphy of the KWV-01 core can be correlated to that of the southwest Karoo Basin. In doing so,
the KWV3n normal polarity magnetozone in the upper Fort Brown to lower Koonap formations can be correlated
to the N2 normal polarity magnetozone identified by Lanci et al. (2013) within the Abrahamskraal Formation
at Ouberg Pass (Figure 12). The thin KWV2n normal polarity magnetozone in the middle of the Fort Brown

Figure 12. Magnetostratigraphic and lithostratigraphic correlation between the southwest and southeast Karoo Basin and the Permian composite reference

Formation would then correlate to N3 identified by Lanci et al. (2013) in the Waterford Formation (Figure 12).
Correlation of normal polarity sub zones (i.e., KWV1r.3n, KWV1r.2n, and KWV1r.1n) is less obvious, but we
suggest a correlation of the normal polarity zone within the Tierberg Formation (Abubakre & De Kock, 2021)
at the top of borehole KZF-01 to KWV1r.1n (Figure 12). Two normal polarity magnetozones at the top of the
Collingham Formation and base of the Prince Albert Formation in KZF-01 (Abubakre & De Kock, 2021) are not
identified in KWV-01.
The normal polarity magnetozone KWV3n at the top of the KWV-01 core is interpreted to mark the onset
of the Illawarra mixed polarity interval at the top of the Kiaman Reverse Polarity Superchron (i.e., GU1n).
The end-Kiaman is placed at or near the base of the Capitanian, but the precise age was not well constrained
(Hounslow & Balabanov, 2018; Menning et al., 2006; Steiner, 2006). Recently, Belica, Tohver, Pisarevsky,
et al. (2017) constrained the end-Kiaman (i.e., the so-called Illawarra reversal) to be between 265.05 ± 0.35 Ma

### page_21
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2022JB024384
(Ar-Ar on plagioclase) and 263.51 ± 0.05 Ma (U-Pb thermal ionization mass spectrometry or TIMS age by
Metcalfe et al. [2015]). Lanci et al. (2013) reported U-Pb sensitive high-resolution ion microprobe or SHRIMP
zircon ages from tuffaceous units at Ouberg Pass within the Illawarra mixed polarity interval of between 264 and
268 Ma, while McKay et al. (2015) reported a U-Pb SHRIMP zircon ages of 260.6 ± 8.9 Ma 264.7 ± 2.5 Ma
from the Abrahamskraal Formation. Lanci et al. (2022) presented a cyclostratigraphic calibration combined with
radiometric ages and reported a 266.5 ± 0.26 Ma age for the end-Kiaman at Ouberg Pass (i.e., start of GU1n).
The Tierberg, Kookfontein, and much of the Waterford formations of the Ecca Group in the southwestern part
of the basin are characterized by dominantly reversed magnetic polarity, with a normal polarity magnetozone in
the middle of the Tierberg Formation reported from the top of the KWZ-01 core and several poorly constrained
normal polarity subzones in the Kookfontein, Skoorsteenberg, and lower Tierberg formations (Abubakre &
De Kock, 2021; Belica, Tohver, Flint, et al., 2017). Belica, Tohver, Flint, et al. (2017) correlated poorly char-
acterized normal polarity subzones from core OR1 and Pienaarsfontein to Kungurian normal polarity zones of
the Geomagnetic Polarity Time Scale (i.e., Cl3n). Such a correlation is, however, not compatible with U-Pb
SHRIMP zircon ages of 269.5 ± 1.2 and 270.4 ± 2.7 Ma reported by Belica, Tohver, Flint, et al. (2017) and
McKay et al. (2016) from the Tierberg Formation. Here we suggest a correlation of the normal polarity magne-
tozone in the middle of the Tierberg Formation of Abubakre and De Kock (2021) to the late Roadian normal
polarity magnetozone in the reference composite of Hounslow and Balabanov (2018), which would account for
the reported U-Pb SHRIMP zircon ages (i.e., Cl3r.n1). In the KWV-01 core, this can potentially be correlated to
normal polarity subzone KWV1r.1n in the Trumpeters Member of the Rippon Formation (Figure 12). The depo-
sition of Prince Albert, Whitehill, and Collingham formations are constrained between ∼282 Ma to ∼270 Ma by
U-Pb SHRIMP zircon ages from tuffaceous units in the southwest (Griffis et al., 2019; Turner, 1999). Abubakre
and De Kock (2021) thus correlated two short normal polarity subzones in the KZF-01 core to Kungurian normal
polarity zones (i.e., Cl3n and Cl2n) in the reference composite of Hounslow and Balabanov (2018). Equivalent
normal polarity zones or subzones are not well-defined in the lower section of the KWV-01 core, but Cl2n could
potentially be represented by KWV1r.1n in the KWV-01 core. The identification of short normal polarity zones
within the Kiaman Reverse Superchron, however, is controversial. The identification of such short normal polar-
ity magnetozones in the KWV-01 core could cement the existence of such magnetozones, but there is currently
too much uncertainty surrounding the age and correlation of these in the KWV-01 core (e.g., future geochro-
nology could reveal that the KWV1r.1n to KWV2 section is best correlated to the short polarity magnetozones
immediately before the onset of GU1n).
The top of the KWV-01 core in the Koonap Formation is constrained to be near 263 Ma, while the top of the Ecca
Group in the KWV-01 core was deposited during an early Capitanian normal polarity zone between 264 Ma and
265 Ma. Deposition of the Ecca Group likely commenced around ∼281 Ma (Figure 12). As such drillcore from
KWV-01 span 18 million years of deposition of which the Ecca Group represents ∼16 million years. From the
magnetostratigraphic correlation, the lithostratigraphic boundary between the Ecca and Beaufort groups is shown
to be time transgressive. The boundary represents a change from marine to terrestrial facies and has long been
interpreted as diachronous and to young from the southwest to the north based on sedimentology and biostratigra-
phy (Catuneanu et al., 2002; Rubidge, 2005; Rubidge et al., 1999). Here, the age of the boundary can be precisely
calibrated. At Ouberg Pass in the southwest (Figure 1), the end-Kiaman is dated at 266.5 ± 0.26 Ma (Lanci
et al., 2022). The base of the Beaufort Group at Ouberg Pass occurs 138.9 m below this (Lanci et al., 2013). The
base of the Beaufort Group at Ouberg Pass can thus be dated at 267.4 ± 0.26 Ma assuming a constant sedimenta-
tion rate of 16 cm/kyr (Lanci et al., 2022). In KWV-01, the same lithological boundary falls within the middle part
the KWV3 normal polarity magnetozone (i.e., correlated to GU1n; Figure 12) and corresponds to the middle of
polarity magnetozone N2 at Ouberg Pass (∼27 m above the end-Kiaman) with an age of 266.3 ± 0.26 Ma, using
the astronomically calibrated age model of Lanci et al. (2022). This indicates ∼1.1 million years of diachronism.
6. Conclusions
The Permian rocks of the southeast Karoo Basin in core from KWV-01 reveal dual polarity primary rema-
nence components (components B- and B+) that pass quality C reversals test as well as baked contact tests
where the rocks are in contact with KLIP dolerite intrusions. These intrusions have affected some of the lithol-
ogies in the KWV-01 core magnetically, and likely caused acquisition of a lower stability north-up remanence
(component A), but without obscuring the higher stability Permian primary remanence. The A component is

indistinguishable from magnetizations recorded by dolerite specimens (i.e., component DOL). The combined B
±paleomagnetic pole compares favorably with previously published paleopoles from the Ecca Group and lower
Beaufort Group. Sedimentary rocks in core from KWV-01 record predominantly B+ magnetizations representing
the Kiaman Reverse Polarity Superchron. B− magnetizations define three normal polarity zones in the lower
Koonap, Waterford, and Ford Brown formations in the upper parts of the KWV-01 core, representing the Illa-
warra mixed polarity interval. As such, the end Kiaman is recorded in the KWV-01 core and can be correlated to
the southwest section of the basin, where it is recorded at Ouberg Pass. Correlation between KWV-01 and Ouberg
Pass suggests an age of 266.3 ± 0.26 Ma for the boundary between the Ecca and the Beaufort groups at KWV-01,
and 267.4 ± 0.26 Ma at Ouberg Pass, thus calibrating this diachronous boundary in the south of the Karoo Basin
for the first time at 1.1 million years.
Data Availability Statement
The electrical dip meter log for KWV-01, details of core orientation, all demagnetization data, least-squares
fits as well as rock magnetic data used to create this manuscript are available at http://dx.doi.org/10.17632/
f7p753f2hp.1. Least-squares analysis of demagnetization data, orthogonal diagrams, equal-area nets, and J/Jo
diagrams was made using PaleoMag 3.2 (Jones, 2002), available at http://cires1.colorado.edu/people/jones.craig/
PMag3.html. Paleopoles were visualized using GPlates 2.2 (Williams et al., 2012), available at https://www.
gplates.org/. IRM acquisition curves were unmixed using the MAX Unmix software (Maxbauer et al., 2016)
through the online application available at http://shinyapps.its.carleton.edu/max-unmix/.
